name: Kimeru, Tiania

catalog_citation: Hyman, Larry M. & Mwaambi G. Mbûûi. 2022. Dahl's law and g-deletion in Tiania: A dialect of Kimeru (Bantu, Kenya). Language in Africa 3(2): 212-238. doi:10.37892/2686-8946-2022-3-2-212-238 (open PDF, iling-ran.ru). Corroboration: Ford, Kevin C. 1976. Tone in Kikamba and the Central Kenya Bantu languages. Studies in African Linguistics 7(3): 261-293.
catalog_locator: p. 214 n. 2 (PDF p. 3) and p. 221 n. 5 (PDF p. 10); Ford 1976 p. 261 (abstract) and p. 267 (9)
catalog_quote: The Tiania forms here and elsewhere are as pronounced by the second author. H(igh) tone is marked by an acute accent (´) and L(ow) tone is unmarked. A raised H tone is marked with a double acute accent ( ̋), while the symbol ˚ indicates that a prepausal L is realized with a level pitch rather than the default prepausal low fall (cf. Ford 1976). ... With a few exceptions, prepenultimate long vowels are shortened in Tiania: o‑tó-saal-a 'to choose us' vs. o-tó-sal-er-a 'to choose for us'. In addition, a vowel followed by a nasal+consonant (NC) complex lengthens in penultimate position, but not prepenultimately. Hence /tɔng/ 'touch' o-tɔɔnga 'to touch', o-tɔng-an-a 'to touch each other'.
world_status: statement found in an open source

A raised H tone is marked with a double acute accent ( ̋), while the symbol ˚ indicates that a prepausal L is realized with a level pitch rather than the default prepausal low fall (cf. Ford 1976)." In addition, a vowel followed by a nasal+consonant (NC) complex lengthens in penultimate position, but not pr…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Meru is a two-level (H/L) tone language with lexically and grammatically distinctive tone; no source opened states a word-stress rule. The only prominence-related statement is positional: in Tiania long vowels survive only in the penultimate syllable (prepenultimate long vowels shorten; NC-lengthening applies only in the penult), i.e. a penultimate-length effect, not a stress rule. Ford 1976 (p. 261, 267) states that in all Central Kenya Bantu dialects examined, including Imenti, Tigania and Miitine, 'tone is both lexically distinctive and serves to reinforce particular aspects of syntax', with two basic tone levels expandable to four (extra-high/extra-low) at syntactic boundaries.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: Hyman & Mbûûi 2022 n. 5: 'with a few exceptions' prepenultimate long vowels shorten; n. 11 (p. 232): a CVVC root keeps its length before the short habitual -a, suggesting the root syllable counts as penultimate within a smaller domain. Taitumu 2014 (MA thesis on word formation, p. 12) asserts in passing that in a newly coined Kimeru noun 'stress is placed on the first syllable of the new naming unit' (mwitithiangari 'vehicle driver'); this is an unargued illustration of Štekauer's onomasiological model, not a phonological description, and no other source supports initial stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Verb and noun forms in isolation and in sentence context (Tiania); tone marking conventions are at word level with prepausal (utterance-final) effects. Gacunku 2005 (p. 33) explicitly puts tone outside its scope and (pp. 230-231) treats penultimate accent only as an untested hypothesis borrowed from Meinhof 1932. Kanana Erastus 2011 describes segments and vowel length of six dialects but is silent on tone and stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes Tiania (= Tigania, Glottolog dialect tiga1244), one of the six dialects Glottolog lists under meru1245, from the speech of co-author Mbûûi (Ming'ong'ine village, Tiania West). Ford 1976 independently confirms lexical tone for Imenti (imen1238), Tigania (tiga1244) and Miitine (miut1238) with named informants. Note: PHOIBLE's 'Kimeru (GM 1641)' inventory mapped to meru1245 cites Rubanza 2008 'Kimeru' (Languages of Tanzania Project) = Meru of Tanzania (Rwa), a different language; do not treat it as a meru1245 source.

new_statements.quote: High tone is marked with an acute accent and low tone is unmarked. The symbol ˚ indicates a low tone with level pitch which contrasts only before pause with the more common low tone with falling pitch. ( ̋ ) marks superhigh tone.
new_statements.citation: Hyman, Larry M. & Mwaambi G. Mbûûi. 2024. Diminutivization and expressive lateralization in Tiania. Morphology 34.
new_statements.locator: footnote 5, attached to the sentence 'Table 2 exemplifies stem /r/ → [l] in each noun class.' in section 2 'Expressive lateralization' (article pages 489-518; the HTML rendering shows no page numbers, so the exact page of the footnote is not determinable from what was opened)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: No file exists held by the project for this work, as the reader stated: my own two automated download attempts (PDF URL and article URL, browser user readers) both returned the same 3038-byte Springer 'Client Challenge' bot page (discarded). I refetched from the open_url through the download tool (Springer -> idp.springer.com cookie redirect -> article HTML) and ran three independent extraction passes. Footnote 5 is present verbatim exactly as quoted: 'High tone is marked with an acute accent and low tone is unmarked. The symbol ˚ indicates a low tone with level pitch which contrasts only before pause with the more common low tone with falling pitch. ( ̋) marks superhigh tone.', attached to…
new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the existing statement from Hyman & Mbûûi 2022 (tone language, no stress statement): the 2024 paper repeats the 2022 tone-marking convention in its footnote 5 (with the addition of a superhigh-tone diacritic) and adds nothing on stress or penultimate prominence; it refers the reader to Hyman and Mbûûi (2022) for Dahl's law (footnote 3). Note the listed citation says 'Morphology 34'; CrossRef gives volume 35, issue 4, pp. 489-518 (online 5 Nov 2024). The quote was obtained through the download tool's rendering of the article HTML and was identical across two independent extraction passes, but I could not inspect the raw HTML or PDF myself.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The paper treats Tiania as a tone language (H marked by acute, L unmarked, a prepausal level-L diacritic, and a superhigh tone) and says nothing about word stress or prominence; the words stress, prominence and penultimate do not occur anywhere in the body, footnotes, tables or appendices. The only length remarks are segmental (a long vowel in diminutive forms such as /ka-o-/ realized as [kɔ:] in section 3.12, and a long vowel before trilled [r] in Appendix 2), not prominence statements.
new_statements.exceptions: none (the paper is about diminutive noun-class morphology and r/l lateralization, not prosody)
new_statements.identity_note: The work describes Tiania [e-tianíá], a speech variety of Kimeru spoken in Kenya, which is exactly the variety the catalog item meru1245 ('Kimeru, Tiania') names; it is not the Tanzanian Meru (Rwa) that some search hits in this folder refer to.

sources.citation: Ford, Kevin C. 1976. Tone in Kikamba and the Central Kenya Bantu languages. Studies in African Linguistics 7(3): 261-293.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No stress statement. p. 261: 'In all the dialects, tone is both lexically distinctive and serves to reinforce particular aspects of syntax'; dialects examined include Imenti, Tigania, Miitine (Meru), Mwimbi, Muthambi, Cuka, Tharaka, Embu, Mbeere, Kikuyu, Kikamba, with named informants (p. 262 n. 1). p. 267 (9): noun tonal classes by final tone: Tigania 5 classes, Miitine and one Imenti speaker 4, Tharaka and another Imenti speaker 3. Penultimate gliding rules (pp. 266-267) are stated for Kikamba only.
